title: What happens to patients when a cyber attack disrupts NHS tests?
summary: When the June 2024 attack on pathology supplier Synnovis sharply reduced testing capacity, NHS teams prioritised urgent samples, used other laboratories and postponed care that depended on results. In the 26 September update, provisional figures showed 10,152 acute outpatient appointments and 1,710 elective procedures postponed at two London trusts.

journey.title: From a test request to a treatment decision during disruption

steps.label: Send the specimen for testing
steps.text: A clinician orders a pathology test and relies on the result for decisions such as diagnosis, preparation for surgery or blood transfusion. Shared laboratories handle testing for several organisations.

note.heading: Why disruption spreads
note.text: Synnovis is a pathology partnership serving more than one trust and other organisations. Shared provision means a supplier outage can affect several clinical pathways at the same time.

steps.label: Keep urgent care moving
steps.text: Prioritise urgent samples, coordinate spare capacity with other laboratories and divert work where needed. Some operations also depend on a safe match for blood products and may have to be postponed.

steps.label: Bring testing and reporting back in stages
steps.text: Rebuild the testing and reporting services and bring back work as capacity returns. NHS England reported that nearly all services were operating in early October 2024 and later confirmed full restoration by December 2024.

steps.label: Rebook affected patients and review harm
steps.text: Follow each affected appointment or procedure through to treatment or another clinical decision. Clinical harm and the investigation into stolen data require separate follow-up.

postponed.title: Two trusts reported 10,152 acute appointments and 1,710 procedures postponed
postponed.description: Cumulative since 3 June, as reported by NHS England London on 26 September 2024.
postponed.note: NHS England labelled these figures provisional and based on unvalidated trust management information. Some patients may have had more than one affected appointment or procedure.

recovery.title: The cumulative outpatient count rose more slowly in the later updates
recovery.description: Selected NHS England updates for the same two trusts from 11 July to 26 September 2024.
recovery.note: Unevenly spaced snapshots. The chart does not show whether previously postponed appointments had taken place.

testing-capacity.title: Testing capacity can become the bottleneck for treatment
testing-capacity.text: With sharply reduced test processing after the attack, trusts had to prioritise urgent work and seek mutual aid from other laboratories. At the two most affected trusts the provisional weekly figures recorded 814 elective procedures postponed on 3 to 9 June 2024 and five on 16 to 22 September. NHS England also recorded diversion of donated organs for use by other trusts.
testing-capacity.evidenceGap: Published figures capture disruptions at the two main trusts. They do not provide a reconciled count of affected people across the whole system.
testing-capacity.measure: Measure time from sample to usable result by clinical urgency throughout an outage, including samples diverted to other labs.

improvement.title: Coordinate mutual aid and restore core testing
improvement.status: NHS England reported mutual aid with other laboratories in June, near-complete service restoration in October and full restoration by December 2024.

consequences.text: People waiting for diagnosis, surgery or another procedure could have their care delayed. The minister’s answer records that in one case the attack contributed to a patient’s death. This case documents one severe consequence of the incident. A harm rate would require the number of affected patients and consistent follow-up.

clearance.title: Restored testing does not by itself tell patients when postponed care will happen
clearance.text: The cumulative number of acute outpatient appointments postponed rose from 6,199 in the 11 July update to 10,083 in the 22 August update. It then rose by 69 to 10,152 in the 26 September update. This records the slowing addition of postponements, while the restoration update describes which services were operating.
clearance.evidenceGap: The published totals do not follow the postponed cohort through to completed treatment, quantify the extra waiting time for each patient or establish a rate of lasting harm.
clearance.measure: Track time from postponement to completed care or changed clinical plan, with harm reviews by clinical priority and affected service.

consequences.text: In the weekly updates a number of postponed elective procedures were cancer treatments. For those patients the time to rebook and deliver treatment matters as well as the number of tests the laboratory can run.

supplier-assurance.question: What changed in how the NHS checks supplier resilience after Synnovis?
supplier-assurance.answer: Alex Mayer asked what steps had been taken. The Department described the difficulty of tracking dependencies across more than 80,000 suppliers, set out assurance work and linked it to the health and social care cybersecurity strategy and proposed legislation.
supplier-assurance.watch: Look for evidence of supplier coverage and successful continuity exercises, including access to spare laboratory capacity and realistic time to restore critical tests.

takeaways.label: The handoff
takeaways.text: A blood test delay can delay a decision in a clinic or operating theatre even when that department stays open.

takeaways.label: The disruption
takeaways.text: Two south-east London trusts reported more than 11,000 combined postponements in the September 2024 figures. A minister later confirmed that the incident contributed to the death of a patient.

takeaways.label: What to watch
takeaways.text: Ask whether suppliers and trusts can show that urgent testing would keep running if a shared service went down again.

how-it-works.heading: Care disruption and data exposure affect different groups
how-it-works.text: The NHS’s 2025 questions and answers distinguishes interruption to care from the data breach. Appointment cancellations were confined to south-east London, while the investigation into stolen files could relate to service users beyond those trusts.

outcomes.heading: Service recovery and patient recovery
outcomes.text: In September 2024, NHS England reported that GPs could again access the full range of pathology tests. It also said a backlog of non-urgent primary care tests still needed attention. Its later account said services were fully restored by December 2024. To measure recovery for patients, follow each postponed case through to a result and treatment decision, including the clinical effect of the delay.

outcomes.heading: What the incident can establish
outcomes.text: The case establishes that disruption at a shared supplier can cause downstream delays and serious harm. It gives no comparison of patient outcomes in comparable incidents with and without a particular resilience measure.

cost-and-funding.heading: Where recovery costs fall
cost-and-funding.text: Recovery included work at the supplier, mutual aid at other laboratories, clinical rescheduling and follow-up. The NHS updates and parliamentary answers cited here do not provide a reconciled cost across those organisations or a unit cost per affected patient.

whats-changing.heading: Patient notifications continued after testing recovered
whats-changing.text: In August 2026, West Suffolk NHS Foundation Trust said it had written to around 70 patients whose data was affected. This was a local follow-up to the data breach. It measures notification at one trust and is separate from the figures for delayed care in south-east London.

whats-changing.heading: What to look for after the Bill
whats-changing.text: Parliament continued considering the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill in November 2026. Track the final requirements and then the results of practical exercises showing whether critical services and their suppliers can maintain care during disruption.
